newsitem.title: USA: SEC still weighing U.S. derivatives rules.
newsitem.headline: SEC still weighing U.S. derivatives rules.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission is still considering changes to its derivatives disclosure proposal and may not release final rules this year, a commission official said.

"It's a top priority of the commission," deputy chief accountant Stephen Swad told reporters after a speech here. The SEC staff is "hoping to get to the commission by the end of the year" with a revised proposal that would then have to be approved by the commissioners, Swad said.
Under a December SEC proposal, companies would have to disclose more about use of derivatives than under current law.

The SEC proposed three possible disclosure formats, including a tabular presentation of derivatives use, an analysis of positions' sensitivity to various market moves, and use of quantitative figures such as "value at risk."
The SEC staff has not yet formed a consensus about how the proposal should be revised, if at all, Swad said.
"People think that there's a preconceived notion about what the end product is," Swad said. "I would know that, if anyone would know that, and I don't know."
The proposal could be redrafted or the staff could recommend not to go forward, Swad said.
"There's no telling what we'll do," Swad said. "I should not communicate that there is a probable outcome because there absolutely is not."
Swad praised efforts by the Financial Accounting Standards Board to revise accounting procedures for derivatives.

"We're super-supportive of their private sector standards-setting process," Swad said. "As it relates to their exposure draft (on derivatives), I think we believe that it's a step in the right direction."
FASB released its draft proposal for comment in June.
Under the proposal, all derivatives would be carried on a company's balance sheet, unlike the present treatment where some derivatives are listed off-balance-sheet.
The proposal would also limit the use of hedge accounting, forcing companies to sometimes report fluctuations in the value of derivatives holdings in their net income.

"It comprehensively addresses the accounting for derivatives and that's an improvement," Swad said. "It's a step in the right direction in that it requires fair value of derivatives to be recognized on the balance sheet."
